title: Vayikra: the poor person's flour (Leviticus 2:1)
hookLine: for the flour offering the text says "soul"; Rashi: the poor person gives their very soul

lines: A BULL, A SHEEP, A BIRD.
A WORD CHAPTER ONE NEVER USED.
cards: Chapter one of Leviticus is all animals: a bull from the herd, a sheep or a goat from the flock, or a bird, a turtledove or a young pigeon. Then chapter two opens with something much humbler.
A bowl of fine flour, a little oil poured over it, a pinch of frankincense on top. The kind of thing anyone with a kitchen could bring.
And the very first verse about this simple flour uses a word chapter one never used for the people bringing animals.

teach.b: The verse reads, "And when any one bringeth a meal-offering unto the LORD." But the Hebrew doesn't really say any one.
It says nefesh: a soul. When a soul brings a meal offering. For the animals in chapter one, the text says adam, a person.
Why does the flour get the soul? Rashi, drawing on the Talmud, answers: who usually brings a meal offering? The poor person, who can't afford an animal.
And God says, as it were: I will count it as if he offered his very soul. In that reading, the less you have, the more of you is in what you give. A midrash makes it concrete.
A woman brings a handful of flour to the Temple, and the priest looks down on it: what is there in this to eat, and what is there to offer?
That night he dreams: don't despise her. It's as if she offered her soul. And the Mishnah, at the end of its tractate on meal offerings, gives a line still quoted today.
Of the offerings of an animal, a bird and flour, it says: it's the same whether a person gives much or gives little, as long as they direct their heart to heaven.
In the Mishnah's reading, the gifts aren't ranked by price.

how: The Mishnah's teaching that much or little is the same, if the heart is directed to heaven, is often cited in Jewish teaching about charity and prayer.

and He called: Leviticus's Hebrew name
fine flour: the poor person's offering

games.q: what's inside the offering — tap the pairs.
p: the poor bring their very soul

s: a cheap offering counts for less than an expensive one
the Mishnah says much or little is the same, if the heart is directed to heaven.
the Hebrew of Leviticus 2:1 uses the word for soul
nefesh: when a soul brings a meal offering.
the meal offering was only for priests

games.q: you're a priest in the Temple. a poor woman brings a single handful of flour. what does the midrash say you should do?
o: accept it, but quietly suggest she bring more next time.
treat it as if she had offered her soul.
turn it away: it isn't enough to offer.
games.why: in the midrash the priest scorns it, then dreams: don't despise her. it's as if she offered her soul.

practice: Think of one small thing you could give: a call to someone lonely, a note, ten minutes of real attention, a share of what's in your kitchen.
Picture giving it with your whole attention, the way Rashi says the poor person's flour carries the giver's very soul. Let it be enough, exactly as it is.

wordCard.voice: Vayikra. And He called. The book where a bowl of flour brought by a poor person is described with the word for soul.

orig.note: Hebrew: soul or life, the word Leviticus 2:1 uses for the one who brings flour.

carryVoice: Your line: the poor bring their soul. A handful of flour can carry a whole person. Until tomorrow.
